name: Best square block on a heat map
brief:
`grid` is a heat map of whole-number scores with `R` rows and `C` columns, and scores may be negative. A block is an `s` by `s` square of neighbouring cells. Return the largest total of any block.

Write `best_block_sum(grid, s)`.

Example. In `[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]` with `s = 2` the four blocks total 12, 16, 24 and 28. The answer is 28.
constraints: $1 \le R, C \le 500$ and $1 \le s \le \min(R, C)$. Each score lies between $-10^6$ and $10^6$.
$O(RC)$ time is the target. Adding up each block cell by cell is too slow when `s` is large.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Build a table `P` with one extra row and column, where `P[r][c]` is the sum of every cell above and left of `(r, c)`. Any block total is then four lookups.

examples.note: The bottom-right block holds 5, 6, 8 and 9, which total 28.
Every score is negative, so the best single cell is -1.

tests.call: best_block_sum([[(r * 31 + c * 17) % 201 - 100 for c in range(300)] for r in range(300)], 150)
best_block_sum([[(r * 13 + c * 29) % 1001 - 500 for c in range(500)] for r in range(500)], 167)
best_block_sum([[(r * c) % 7 - 3 for c in range(300)] for r in range(300)], 1)
best_block_sum([[-(r + c) for c in range(250)] for r in range(300)], 200)

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: A prefix table turns any block total into four lookups.
Scores can all be negative, so the best total must not start at 0.
Building the table and scanning every corner both take $O(RC)$.

planted.slip: It starts the best total at 0, so a map of negative scores returns 0.
Its loops stop one short, so blocks touching the last row or column are never tried.
It adds up each block afresh, which is $O(RCs^2)$ and too slow for a large block.
Starting the best total at -10^9 returns a figure too high when every block total is lower.
